title: HTML Document Structure
summary: A basic HTML document has a head for page information and a body for visible content.

subtopics.title: The document frame
subtopics.explanation: `<!doctype html>` tells the browser to use modern HTML rules. It is a declaration at the start of the file, not visible page content. It helps the browser avoid legacy rendering modes. Place it before the `<html>` element so the document begins predictably. The doctype helps select standards mode. Think of it as a sign at a building entrance that tells visitors which rules apply.

subtopics.title: Important pieces
subtopics.explanation: The `<html>` element wraps the whole document and can identify its language with a `lang` attribute. For example, use `lang="en"` for an English page. The language helps assistive technology choose pronunciation rules and helps other tools interpret the content. The root language should reflect the page’s primary language. If a passage changes language, mark that section when pronunciation needs to change. The html element is like a book cover that holds every page.

subtopics.title: Page information
subtopics.explanation: The `<head>` holds metadata, such as the title, character encoding, viewport, and links to stylesheets. Most head contents are not shown as the article itself. Declare UTF-8 so punctuation and international text decode correctly, and include a viewport setting for mobile layouts. Metadata belongs in the head, while readable content belongs in the body. This separation makes page structure and browser settings easier to locate. The head is like a catalog card that describes the book before it is opened.

subtopics.title: Content structure
subtopics.explanation: The `<body>` contains visible page content, such as headings, paragraphs, forms, and controls. Keep the main content here and use elements whose meaning matches their role. This separation helps browsers and assistive tools distinguish document setup from the page people read and use. Use semantic elements inside the body for headings, navigation, forms, and main content. The body is not a reason to put every item in a generic div. The body is like the readable pages inside the cover.

subtopics.title: Good habits
subtopics.explanation: `<title>` names the document in browser tabs, history, and bookmarks. It is different from the visible page heading. Give each page a concise, accurate title so people can distinguish open tabs and identify a page after saving it. Title text is used outside the visible page, so make it useful in tabs and history. Keep the visible h1 clear for people reading the page itself. The title is like a label on a book spine that helps find it later.

foundations.overview: An HTML document has a standard outer structure that tells the browser how to read the page. The document type declaration, root element, head, and body each have a role. Think of them as a book cover, metadata page, and readable chapters. A clear structure supports browsers, search tools, and assistive technology.
foundations.whyItMatters: A reliable document skeleton gives browsers and assistive technology consistent information. It separates page metadata from the content people read and use.
foundations.mentalModel: An HTML document has a standard outer structure that tells the browser how to read the page.
commonUseCases: Set the page language so assistive technology can pronounce its content.
Place the page title and character encoding in the document head.
Keep visible headings, forms, and links in the body.
Create the starting file for a new page.
Add page language, title, and character encoding.
Separate visible content from document metadata.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The head is where page headings belong.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The head stores document metadata; visible page content belongs in the body.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A browser repair means malformed HTML is harmless.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Browsers may build a different tree than intended, affecting layout, scripts, and accessibility.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The title tag is the same as the visible h1.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The title appears in tabs and metadata; the h1 is visible page content and they can serve different purposes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser tab title is the same thing as the page h1.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The title identifies the document outside the page; the h1 labels its visible main content.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A document without a doctype is interpreted the same way everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The doctype helps browsers use standards mode rather than legacy layout behavior.

visualExplorer.title: The document skeleton as a tree
visualExplorer.caption: html is the root; head (metadata) and body (visible content) are its two children, and your content nests inside body.

interactiveExamples.title: The full boilerplate
interactiveExamples.explanation: Here is the complete, correct skeleton every page should start with. Notice the metadata lives in head and the visible content lives in body.

files.index.html:
Hello, structured world!

This content lives in the body.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A page showing the heading 'Hello, structured world!' and a paragraph; the head metadata sets the tab title to 'My First Page' but is not shown in the content.

interactiveExamples.title: Head metadata is invisible
interactiveExamples.explanation: Anything you put in the head — like the title or meta tags — does not appear in the content area. Only body content is rendered.

files.index.html: Only this paragraph is visible.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Just one visible paragraph reading 'Only this paragraph is visible.' — the title text appears in the browser tab, not on the page.

codeLab.title: Build the boilerplate from scratch
codeLab.instructions: This file has only a body of content. Wrap it in a complete, valid document: add the doctype, the html element with lang="en", a head containing charset, viewport, and a <title> of 'About Me', and keep the content inside body.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A fully valid HTML document with the heading and paragraph in the body and 'About Me' as the tab title.

files.index.html:
About Me

I am learning HTML structure.

hints: The doctype <!DOCTYPE html> goes on the very first line.
charset, viewport, and title all belong inside <head>; the heading and paragraph stay in <body>.

keyTakeaways: `<!doctype html>` tells the browser to use modern HTML rules.
The `<html>` element wraps the whole document and can identify its language with a `lang` attribute.
The `<head>` holds metadata, such as the title, character encoding, viewport, and links to stylesheets.
The `<body>` contains visible page content, such as headings, paragraphs, forms, and controls.
`<title>` names the document in browser tabs, history, and bookmarks.
